transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me today, I really appreciate you fitting me in. 

Um... I guess I'm here because... well, it's a little embarrassing to admit, honestly, especially being a psychologist myself. I know exactly how this sounds, and I'm sure it's just my mind playing tricks on me from stress, right? But I came in because I keep hearing Garrett’s voice. 

It's just... it's as clear as if he’s standing right behind me when I'm out on the trail, or when I'm in my painting room. And even though the rational part of me knows he’s dead, in the moment, it just feels completely real. I hope it's okay that I came in for this... does that make sense?
How long have you been hearing Garrett's voice?

Um... well, it hasn't been that long, really. Just... about a month. That's when Garrett died. So I guess this whole... crisis, or whatever you want to call it, has been unfolding since then. 

I mean, it's only been four weeks, so I'm sure it's just a normal part of the grieving process, right? I know acute grief can do strange things to the brain. I really hope I'm not overreacting or taking up your time with something that's just a standard grief response. Am I giving you the right kind of information so far?
Does Garrett's voice you hear ever tell you to do something or is it more like a conversation or just his presence?

Oh, um... no, he definitely doesn't tell me to do anything. I know that would be a much bigger concern, so I want to assure you it's nothing dangerous or scary like that. 

It's really just... well, like I was saying before, it's more about his presence and just... talking. When I'm out on the trail or sitting in my painting room, it's just like he's standing right behind me, maybe commenting on my brushstrokes or just saying my name. It's very conversational. And... I know I already said this, but even though that rational, professional part of my brain knows he's gone, in that split second, the experience feels completely, one-hundred-percent real to me. 

I'm sorry if I'm repeating myself, I just want to make sure I'm giving you an accurate picture. I'm trying to be as helpful as possible. Does that... does that sound like a typical severe grief reaction to you?
Does hearing Garrett's voice cause you any distress or interfere with your daily activities?

Well, um... I guess... I guess it has, a little bit. I mean, I really tried to keep everything normal. I wanted to just push through it, you know? But... well, I suppose it's gotten a bit out of hand. 

I actually... I had to cancel some of my patient sessions. Which I feel terrible about, I really pride myself on being reliable for my clients. And my documentation is a bit... well, it's pretty far behind right now. I just found I couldn't really focus, and I worried I wasn't practicing safely. I didn't want my own issues to impact my patients, I hope you understand that.

And, um... things at home got a little overwhelming, too. My wife actually... she ended up calling crisis services. I think she was just being overly cautious, but... I did feel like I couldn't really trust myself alone. That's actually how I ended up being admitted to the hospital. It just felt like everything—my work, my home life, my safety—it all just sort of... stopped functioning for a minute. 

I'm really embarrassed to admit all that, especially to another professional. I know I should have handled it better. Does that make sense, though? Have you seen other people struggle to keep up with work when they're dealing with something like this?
Do you ever think that Garrett is actually physically present with you when you hear his voice?

Well... yes. I know I sort of mentioned this a second ago, and I really hope it doesn't make me sound... well, too unstable. Because obviously, the logical, clinical part of my brain knows he passed away. But... yes. When it happens, his voice is just so clear. It really does feel like he is physically right there with me. 

Like, if I just turned my head, he'd be standing right behind me in the painting room, or walking right next to me on the trail. In those moments, it just feels completely, absolutely real. Like a true physical presence. I do try to catch myself and use my reality-testing skills right after, I promise. I try to ground myself. Does that... I mean, is that something you see often with acute grief? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture without making you think I'm completely detached from reality.
Have you been feeling sad or depressed most of the time since Garrett passed away?

Well, um... not exactly. I mean, I know that would make sense, right? With him passing away and everything, you'd expect me to just be... devastated and crying all the time. But honestly, I haven't really felt sad or depressed like that. 

I actually felt... well, I've had a lot of energy. A lot of drive. I've been doing a ton of painting, and I've just felt really connected to him, you know? It hasn't been this heavy, dark depression that you might read about in a textbook for grief. It's been more... active, I guess. 

I hope that doesn't sound like I didn't care about him, or like I'm not grieving properly. I know everyone processes loss differently, right? I just want to be honest with you. Does that... does it make sense that I wouldn't be deeply depressed right now? Is that an okay way to be reacting?
Have you felt a persistent low mood or an inability to experience pleasure in things you normally enjoy since Garrett passed away?

Well, um... I guess... I mean, I did say I had a lot of energy for painting earlier, and that was true for a bit, but... lately, I suppose things have felt a little different. I don't want to sound like I'm complaining or not trying my best to stay engaged, because I really am. 

But... yeah, the things that usually anchor me, they just... they feel a bit flat right now. Like, my painting, playing my guitar, rehearsing at the theater... even sitting with my patients, which I usually find so fulfilling. It's just felt a little unreachable lately. Like I'm just going through the motions of a life that... well, that stopped meaning as much. 

I know I should be pushing myself harder to enjoy things, and I really am trying to use behavioral activation techniques on myself. I don't want you to think I'm just giving up or wallowing. It's just been a little harder to find that spark. Have you found that your other patients sometimes go through phases like this where things just feel a bit... muted? Am I explaining that in a way that makes sense?
Do you think there's a possibility that your experience of Garrett's presence is not just a feeling, but actually real?

Well, um... I mean, when you say "actually real," I know how that sounds. I'm a psychologist, so I know the criteria, and I know that believing he is physically, literally alive and present would be... well, a delusion. And I really, really don't want you to think I've lost touch with reality like that. 

I know, logically, that he's gone. I saw him pass. I went to the funeral. I know he is dead. But... sometimes the feeling is just so strong that... I don't know, maybe a tiny part of me hopes or wonders if his spirit or his energy is actually here? Not like a ghost movie, but just... something real. 

But I know that's probably just my grief talking, right? Just a coping mechanism my brain is using because it misses him so much. I'm not actually crazy, I promise. I know he's not physically breathing in the room. I just... I want to make sure I'm giving you the right answer without making myself sound completely psychotic. Does that make sense? Like, it's just a strong feeling, not a... not a break from reality, right?
Do you believe that Garrett is actually, literally alive?

Well, um... no. No, of course not. I mean, I know he's... he's gone. I really do. 

I know I just said it feels very real sometimes, but I don't want you to think I'm completely out of my mind or anything. I know the difference between a very strong feeling of someone's presence and them actually being alive. I'm a professional, I know what that would mean if I actually believed he was breathing and walking around. 

So, no, I don't believe he's literally alive. I know he passed away. I just... I miss him, and sometimes the grief just makes his memory feel very vivid. That's a normal part of the grieving process, isn't it? To have moments where it just feels like they're still around, even when you know they aren't? I hope I'm making sense and not giving you the wrong impression about where my head is at.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your relationships with others, such as friends or family, since you started hearing Garrett's voice?

Well, um... I guess things have been a little strained, maybe? I mean, I really don't want to make it sound like I've just completely fallen apart or that I'm a burden on my family. I've always prided myself on being the one who holds things together, especially for my wife, and... well, for my patients, too. 

But, um, I suppose... I did have to cancel some patient sessions recently. And I got a little behind on my documentation. I know how unprofessional that sounds, and I feel terrible about it. I just... it got to a point where I didn't feel like I could practice safely, you know? Like I couldn't give them the focus they deserved. 

And at home... well, my wife actually ended up calling crisis services. I think she was just really worried because I told her I didn't entirely trust myself to be alone. I wasn't trying to cause a scene or anything, I promise. But that's how I ended up being admitted to the hospital. It just felt like... like my work, my home life, my safety, it all just sort of... stopped functioning for a minute. 

I'm really trying to get back on track, though. I don't want you to think I'm just giving up on my responsibilities. It's just a temporary setback, right? Have you seen other professionals go through a rough patch like this and bounce back? I just hope I'm not coming across as completely incapable...
Do you think there's a part of you that genuinely believes Garrett is alive, even if it's just for a moment?

Well, um... I guess... I mean, I really want to be careful how I say this, because I know how it sounds, being a psychologist and all. I know he's dead. I really do. But... 

When I hear his voice... it's just so clear. Like, as clear as if he's standing right behind me when I'm out on the trail, or... or when I'm in my painting room. And in those exact moments, when I hear him so clearly... it's like my brain just forgets for a second. In that split second, it feels completely real. Like he's actually right there with me. 

But then I catch myself, you know? I remind myself of reality. It's just... in the moment it happens, the feeling is so overpowering. I'm not crazy for having those split-second reactions, am I? I mean, grief does strange things to the mind, right? I just hope I'm explaining this right and not making it sound like I've completely lost my grip on reality... because I haven't, I promise.
Have you been feeling disconnected from the people around you, like your wife or friends, since Garrett passed away?

Well, um... I wouldn't say disconnected, exactly. I mean, my wife has been incredibly supportive, and I really appreciate everything she's done. I don't want to sound ungrateful or like I'm pushing her away. 

I guess... maybe I've been a little quieter than usual? Just, you know, needing a bit more time to myself to process things. I think that's pretty normal when you're grieving, just needing some space to sort through your thoughts. But I certainly don't feel cut off from people. I still care very much about my wife and my friends. 

I just... I want to make sure I'm handling this the right way, without being a burden to anyone. It makes sense to withdraw just a tiny bit when you're going through a loss, doesn't it? I hope I'm not giving the impression that I'm completely isolating myself, because I'm really trying my best to stay engaged.
Have you been experiencing a lack of interest in activities you normally enjoy most of the time since Garrett passed away?

Well, um... I really wouldn't say I've completely lost interest in everything. I mean, I know how important it is to keep up with hobbies, especially for someone in my profession. I always tell my patients to stay active, so I really try to practice what I preach. 

But... I guess lately, it's just been a little harder to find the energy for them? Like, the things that usually anchor me—my painting, playing my guitar, going to rehearsals at the community theater... even sitting with my patients, which I usually love—they just feel a little... flat right now. Almost unreachable, if that makes sense. It's like I'm just sort of going through the motions of a life that... well, that stopped meaning as much right now. 

I know that sounds terrible, and I really don't want you to think I'm just wallowing in self-pity or giving up on the things I care about. I'm still trying, I really am. It's just a normal part of the grieving process to feel a little numb to things for a while, isn't it? I just hope I'm not coming across as someone who's completely checked out, because I do want to get back to enjoying those things again.
Do you feel like you're observing yourself and the people around you from outside your body?

Well, um... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I know dissociation can happen when people are under extreme stress, but... no, I don't feel like I'm floating above myself or anything like that. 

I'm very present in my body. Maybe a little exhausted, sure, but... definitely still in here. I feel the ground when I walk, you know? I think I'm handling the physical reality of things okay. It's important to stay grounded, and I really make an effort to do that. That's a good sign, right? That I'm staying connected to myself physically, I mean. I just want to be sure I'm giving you an accurate picture of how I'm doing.
Have you ever had an experience like this before, where you heard someone's voice or felt their presence after they passed away?

Well, um... no. No, never. I've never experienced anything quite like this before. Not with anyone else, and honestly, not even with Garrett at first. 

It really only started happening recently, during that... that stretch where I was just so incredibly wired. You know, when I was barely sleeping at all, and I started taking on all those impossible projects? I just felt this intense, overwhelming drive to keep going and going, no matter what time it was. That’s when I started hearing his voice. I had never heard him like that before my mood shifted that way, and it definitely wasn't something that happened during my ordinary, everyday grief. 

I hope that makes sense? I mean, when you factor in the severe lack of sleep and how revved up I was, it's pretty understandable that my mind might play a few tricks on me, right? I really don't want you to think I'm losing my grip on reality or anything like that. It was just a very specific, exhausting stretch of time... that's a reasonable explanation for why it happened then, don't you think?
Have you ever had any other experiences where you questioned what is real and what is not, aside from hearing Garrett's voice?

Well, um... no, not really. I mean, aside from that specific time when I was so sleep-deprived and hearing Garrett, I've always had a pretty firm grasp on reality. 

I know how important it is to stay grounded, especially in my line of work. You really have to be able to trust your own mind, you know? And I do. I haven't seen things that aren't there, or had any strange beliefs or anything like that. That whole experience with his voice was just... it was just a blip, really. An isolated incident brought on by extreme stress and exhaustion. 

I'm usually very rational, very level-headed. I think anyone would agree with that if they knew me. So, no, nothing else like that has happened. I'm definitely not someone who struggles with distinguishing reality from... from imagination, generally speaking. I just want to make sure I'm being clear about that. It's perfectly normal for the mind to get a little confused when it's pushed too hard, isn't it? I just hope I'm explaining this in a way that makes sense and doesn't sound too concerning.
Do you feel like you're emotionally distant from the people around you most of the time?

Well, um... no, I wouldn't say that. I try really hard to be there for my friends and family. I mean, as a psychologist, empathy and connection are basically my whole job, right? So I definitely value being emotionally present. 

I guess... maybe sometimes when I'm really overwhelmed or, you know, when I was working those crazy hours and not sleeping, I might have seemed a little distracted? But I wouldn't call it emotionally distant. I always care about the people in my life, very deeply. I just... sometimes I might not have the energy to show it as well as I should. But I always make an effort to reconnect as soon as I can. 

I think it's pretty normal to need a little space when you're under a lot of pressure, don't you? I just want to be sure you know I'm a very caring person. I really do try my best to be a good friend and colleague. That's the right way to look at it, isn't it?
Have you been feeling hopeless about the future since Garrett passed away?

Well, um... no, not hopeless. I mean, it's been hard, obviously. Losing him was... it was a terrible shock. But I wouldn't say I'm hopeless about the future. 

I've been trying to stay positive, you know? I think it's important to keep looking forward, to honor his memory by living a good life. I have my practice, my patients rely on me, and I take that responsibility very seriously. I try to focus on the good things I still have. 

Of course, there are days when I miss him terribly, and I might feel a bit down, but that's just normal grief, right? Everyone goes through that when they lose a spouse. I really try not to let myself wallow in it or give up hope. I want to be resilient. I think I'm handling it as well as anyone could be expected to, don't you think? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right impression—I'm definitely still looking forward to the future, even if it's different now. That's a healthy way to process things, isn't it?
Have you been feeling sad most of the time since Garrett passed away?

Well, um... no, I wouldn't say I'm sad most of the time. I mean, of course, there's sadness. It's a huge loss. But I wouldn't want you to think I'm just sitting around crying all day or anything like that. 

I really try to keep my spirits up. I think it's so important to maintain a positive outlook, especially for my patients. They need me to be strong and stable, you know? So I make a conscious effort to find joy in the little things and keep myself busy. 

Sure, there are moments when the grief hits me, and I might feel a bit tearful, but it passes. I always bounce back. I think it's perfectly natural to have moments of sadness after losing a husband, don't you? But it definitely doesn't consume my whole day or anything. I'm actually doing pretty well, all things considered. I just want to make sure I'm conveying that properly... that I'm coping in a healthy, normal way. That makes sense, right?
Have you ever had a period of time where you heard Garrett's voice and also had other unusual perceptions or beliefs that you now realize weren't based in reality?

Well, um... I guess... I mean, I wouldn't call them "unusual beliefs" exactly. That makes it sound a bit... extreme, doesn't it? But, um, I suppose there was a time... 

It was only during that really, really wired stretch, you know? The time I mentioned before, when I was barely sleeping and taking on all those impossible projects at work. I just felt so driven, like I had to keep going and going. And that's... that's the only time I started hearing Garrett's voice. 

I want to be clear, I had never heard him like that before. Not ever. And it wasn't just, like, ordinary grief where you imagine what your partner would say. It was... different. But it only happened when my mood was completely shifted and I was running on empty. It wasn't like a permanent thing or anything. 

I just want to make sure you understand it was tied to that specific period of being so overworked and sleepless. That's a pretty normal reaction to extreme stress and lack of sleep, right? I mean, anyone's mind might play a few tricks on them under those conditions, don't you think? I just want to be sure I'm explaining it the right way so you don't think it's something worse than it was.

So, no, I don't believe he's literally alive. I know he passed away. I just... I miss him, and sometimes the grief just makes his memory feel very vivid. That's a normal part of the grieving process, isn't it? To have moments where it just feels like they're still around, even when you know they aren't? I hope I'm making sense and not giving you the wrong impression about where my head is at.
